decision.detail: I stand up from the bed. I don't look at the radio. I pull the coat off the back of the chair, slide my arms in, zip it to the chin. The ticket is in the left breast pocket — I can feel the corner of it through the flannel. I walk out of the room. The lobby is warm. Rita is by the coffee pot. Larry is by the coat-check counter. I walk past both of them. I don't stop. I don't say good morning. I go to the door. The street is cold and blue and the delivery van is still backfiring two blocks down. I walk to the Greyhound stand. The coach is there, engine ticking over, driver checking his mirror. I step up. I sit in the aisle seat, second row. I put my bag under the seat in front of me. I don't look out the window at the hotel. I look at the road ahead. The doors hiss shut. The bus pulls out.
decision.intention: Be in Pittsburgh by five. Be on a bench or a floor or the back of the Greyhound waiting area, asleep by eight, awake at six-forty, at my sister's door at 7:15 with gloves and rolled blankets and coffee money in my pocket. The couch is in Pittsburgh. I am going to Pittsburgh. That is the whole forecast. Nothing else. The ballroom is for someone else. The piano is for someone else. The Rialto is for someone else. I have a ticket and a number I dialed last night and a sister standing in her kitchen holding a spoon. That is enough. That is the whole weather report for Wednesday. I am going to sit in this bus and I am going to get there.
decision.words: Nothing to Rita. Nothing to Larry. I walk past. I don't owe them a forecast.
